spec.title: Example 119: HoldExpiredException replaces the ConflictException of POST /orders with no handler mapping it, a 500 instead of a 409, caught by the throws lines of the boundary contract (B12)
spec.description: The first example of the throws lines and the exception outcomes of a boundary contract (Graph::throws in lib/src/reach.rs, lib/src/failures.rs): under each route jvmcontract now lists the exceptions the handler can throw (throw statements, orElseThrow suppliers and Spring Assert calls in everything it reaches, less what a catch on the path takes without rethrowing) and what each becomes (the @ExceptionHandler that takes it, the controller's own first and then the advices in @Order, with the status it answers; the @ResponseStatus on the exception; the status a ResponseStatusException carries; or a 500), with a ! line for an exception type of the module's own that nothing maps and for two handlers of one type in one advice. The patch adds HoldExpiredException, a RuntimeException carrying the hold id, and throws it from OrderService.place where ConflictException was thrown; ApiErrors is not touched, so Spring answers a 500 from the container's error page instead of the 409 problem detail. The code compiles, the context starts, the unit tests go through the service. The change is a refactoring in the developer's eyes, so the runner regenerates the contract and reports as the violation the new ! line under POST /orders (throws HoldExpiredException: no @ExceptionHandler takes it and it carries no @ResponseStatus, so the response is a 500). The runner compiles the module with Gradle, reads the runtime class path through the build's printRuntimeClasspath task, and runs jvmcontract update then verify with --resources and --classpath; the module's Spring Boot tests need Docker and are recorded as the tests' result.
